questions.body: What will be the output of `'5' - 3` and `'5' + 3` in JavaScript?
questions.keyPoints: Subtraction forces numeric conversion; addition with string triggers string concatenation.

options.explanation: The `-` operator coerces strings to numbers (`5 - 3 = 2`), while `+` with a string operand performs string concatenation (`'5' + 3 = '53'`).
The `+` operator does not convert `'5'` to a number when one operand is a string; it concatenates.

options.text: `NaN` and `'53'`
options.explanation: `'5'` is cleanly parsed to number 5 during subtraction, not NaN.

options.text: `NaN` and `NaN`
options.explanation: Both operations are valid JavaScript expressions yielding a number and string respectively.

questions.body: What does `typeof null` return in JavaScript?
questions.keyPoints: Historical bug in JavaScript where null has type tag 0 corresponding to object.

options.text: `'object'`
options.explanation: Due to a legacy bug in the original JS engine where object type tags were 000 and null was pointer NULL (0x00), `typeof null` returns `'object'`.

options.text: `'null'`
options.explanation: While null is a primitive type, `typeof null` notoriously returns `'object'`.

options.text: `'undefined'`
options.explanation: `typeof undefined` returns `'undefined'`, not null.

options.text: `'primitive'`
options.explanation: `'primitive'` is not a valid return value for the typeof operator.

questions.body: What is the primary characteristic of JavaScript `Symbol` primitive values?
questions.keyPoints: Symbols are unique and immutable identifier tokens.

options.text: Every symbol value returned from `Symbol()` is completely unique and immutable.
options.explanation: Each call to `Symbol()` produces a unique, immutable symbol that can be used as a non-colliding object property key.

options.text: Symbols with the same description string are strictly equal (`Symbol('x') === Symbol('x')`).
options.explanation: The description is purely informative; `Symbol('x') === Symbol('x')` evaluates to false.

options.text: Symbols can be converted to numbers using unary `+` operator.
options.explanation: Converting a Symbol to a number throws a TypeError.

options.text: Symbols are enumerable in standard `for...in` loops.
options.explanation: Symbol keys are non-enumerable in standard `for...in` loops and `Object.keys()`.

questions.body: How does property lookup work across the prototype chain in JavaScript?
questions.keyPoints: JS searches the object itself, then traverses up `[[Prototype]]` until found or null.

options.text: It checks the object's own properties first, then traverses up `__proto__` / `[[Prototype]]` until reaching `Object.prototype`, and finally `null`.
options.explanation: Property lookup checks own properties, then moves up the prototype link until the property is found or `Object.prototype.__proto__` (null) is reached.

options.text: It searches all prototypes concurrently and throws an error if duplicate property names exist.
options.explanation: Property resolution is sequential from bottom to top; shadowing occurs if an own property exists.

options.text: It only checks `Object.prototype` if the object was created using constructor functions.
options.explanation: All standard objects link to `Object.prototype` unless created with `Object.create(null)`.

options.text: It copies all prototype properties onto the child object during instantiation.
options.explanation: Inheritance is delegated via live references, not cloned.

questions.body: What is the difference between `Object.freeze()` and `Object.seal()`?
questions.keyPoints: seal prevents adding/deleting properties; freeze also prevents modifying existing properties (writable: false).

options.text: `Object.seal()` allows modifying values of existing writable properties, while `Object.freeze()` marks existing properties as read-only.
options.explanation: Both prevent addition and deletion of properties, but `freeze()` additionally makes all existing own data properties non-writable.

options.text: `Object.freeze()` prevents prototype changes, while `Object.seal()` allows mutating `__proto__`.
options.explanation: Both methods make the target object non-extensible, preventing prototype re-assignment.

options.text: `Object.freeze()` performs deep freezing recursively on nested objects.
options.explanation: Both `Object.freeze()` and `Object.seal()` are shallow by default.

options.text: `Object.seal()` prevents property deletion while `Object.freeze()` permits deletion.
options.explanation: Neither allows property deletion (`configurable: false`).

questions.body: Which expression correctly evaluates to `true` when testing if variable `x` contains `NaN`?
questions.keyPoints: NaN is not equal to itself; Number.isNaN checks specifically for NaN without coercion.

options.text: `Number.isNaN(x)` or `Object.is(x, NaN)`
options.explanation: `NaN === NaN` is false. `Number.isNaN()` and `Object.is(x, NaN)` reliably verify whether `x` is the value `NaN` without coercive quirks of global `isNaN()`.

options.text: `x === NaN`
options.explanation: According to IEEE 754 floating-point standard, `NaN === NaN` is always false.

options.text: `typeof x === 'NaN'`
options.explanation: `typeof NaN` returns `'number'`.

options.text: `x == null`
options.explanation: `NaN == null` is false; only `null` and `undefined` equal each other with loose equality.

questions.body: What happens when you invoke a standalone function in `'use strict'` mode regarding its `this` binding?
questions.keyPoints: In strict mode, un-bound function calls have this as undefined rather than window/global.

options.text: `this` is `undefined`.
options.explanation: In strict mode, default binding of `this` in standalone function invocations is `undefined` rather than the global `window` object.

options.text: `this` points to `window` or global object.
options.explanation: Defaulting to global object occurs only in non-strict (sloppy) mode.

options.text: A ReferenceError is thrown upon calling the function.
options.explanation: Calling the function is valid; only accessing properties on `this` would throw TypeError.

options.text: `this` points to an empty object `{}`.
options.explanation: `this` is literally `undefined`.

questions.body: How is `this` determined inside an ES6 arrow function?
questions.keyPoints: Arrow functions do not bind their own this; they inherit it lexically.

options.text: Lexically resolved from the enclosing execution context at definition time.
options.explanation: Arrow functions do not possess their own `this`, `arguments`, `super`, or `new.target`; they inherit `this` from the enclosing lexical scope.

options.text: Dynamically bound based on how the function is invoked at runtime.
options.explanation: Dynamic binding applies to regular functions, not arrow functions.

options.text: Bound to the object preceding the dot operator at invocation time.
options.explanation: Arrow functions ignore call-site dot bindings.

options.text: Always bound to the global `window` object.
options.explanation: It depends on the lexical parent context, not fixed to global.

questions.body: What is the primary difference between `Function.prototype.call` and `Function.prototype.apply`?
questions.keyPoints: call takes arguments individually; apply takes an array-like object of arguments.

options.text: `call` accepts arguments individually as a comma-separated list, while `apply` accepts arguments as an array.
options.explanation: `fn.call(ctx, arg1, arg2)` takes separate arguments, whereas `fn.apply(ctx, [arg1, arg2])` passes arguments in an array.

options.text: `call` executes asynchronously while `apply` executes synchronously.
options.explanation: Both execute immediately and synchronously.

options.text: `call` returns a new function while `apply` invokes the function immediately.
options.explanation: `bind` returns a new bound function; both `call` and `apply` invoke immediately.

options.text: `apply` can only be used with constructor functions.
options.explanation: Both work on any standard callable function.

questions.body: Which array method mutates the original array in place?
questions.keyPoints: splice, sort, reverse mutate; map, filter, slice, concat return new arrays.

options.text: `Array.prototype.splice()`
options.explanation: `splice()` modifies the original array by removing or replacing existing elements. Methods like `slice()`, `filter()`, and `map()` return new arrays.

options.text: `Array.prototype.slice()`
options.explanation: `slice()` returns a shallow copy of a portion of an array without mutating the original.

options.text: `Array.prototype.map()`
options.explanation: `map()` generates and returns a new transformed array.

options.text: `Array.prototype.concat()`
options.explanation: `concat()` merges arrays into a new array instance.

questions.keyPoints: JS is pass-by-value where object references are passed by value; reassigning parameter does not reassign caller variable.

options.text: `'Alice'`
options.explanation: Mutating `obj.name = 'Alice'` affects the referenced heap object. Reassigning `obj = { name: 'Bob' }` only alters the local parameter copy of the reference.

options.text: `'Bob'`
options.explanation: Reassigning the formal argument `obj` does not alter the caller's `person` variable.

options.text: `'Charlie'`
options.explanation: `obj.name = 'Alice'` executed before reassignment, altering the property.

options.text: `undefined`
options.explanation: `name` property is set to 'Alice'.

questions.body: In ES6 destructuring, under which specific condition is a default value triggered?
questions.keyPoints: Default values in destructuring are applied only when value is undefined, not null or false.

options.text: Only when the evaluated property value is strictly `undefined`.
options.explanation: Default values in parameter and object destructuring (`{ x = 10 }`) trigger only if the incoming value is `undefined`. If it is `null`, `false`, `0`, or `''`, the default is ignored.

options.text: When the value is falsy (`false`, `0`, `null`, `undefined`, `''`).
options.explanation: Only `undefined` triggers destructuring defaults.

options.text: When the value is either `null` or `undefined`.
options.explanation: `null` does not trigger destructuring defaults; it assigns `null`.

options.text: Only if the property key is entirely absent from the object.
options.explanation: Even if the key is present with value `undefined`, the default value activates.

questions.body: What is the syntactic difference between the Rest parameter and the Spread operator in JavaScript?
questions.keyPoints: Rest collects multiple elements into an array; Spread expands an iterable into individual elements.

options.text: Rest collects multiple remaining elements into a single array, while Spread unpacks elements of an iterable into individual items.
options.explanation: Rest syntax (`...args` in function parameters) condenses multiple elements into an array. Spread syntax expands an array/iterable into arguments or array literals.

options.text: Rest only works on objects, while Spread only works on arrays.
options.explanation: Both operate on iterables and objects.

options.text: Spread can only appear as the last argument in a function declaration.
options.explanation: Rest must be the last parameter; Spread can appear anywhere within an argument list or array literal.

options.text: Rest performs deep cloning while Spread performs shallow cloning.
options.explanation: Spread performs shallow copying; Rest does not copy existing objects.

questions.body: What does `const res = (0 ?? 42)` evaluate to, compared to `const res2 = (0 || 42)`?
questions.keyPoints: Nullish coalescing (??) checks for null/undefined; logical OR (||) checks falsiness.

options.text: `res` is `0` and `res2` is `42`.
options.explanation: `??` only falls back on `null` or `undefined`, so `0 ?? 42` returns `0`. `||` falls back on any falsy value, so `0 || 42` returns `42`.

options.text: `res` is `42` and `res2` is `42`.
options.explanation: `0` is not nullish, so `??` returns `0`.

options.text: `res` is `0` and `res2` is `0`.
options.explanation: `0` is falsy, so `||` moves to the right-hand operand `42`.

options.text: Throws a SyntaxError due to unexpected operator precedence.
options.explanation: Both are valid syntax.

questions.body: Which of the following is a key advantage of ES6 `Map` over standard plain JavaScript objects (`{}`)?
questions.keyPoints: Map keys can be of any data type, retains insertion order, and size property is built-in.

options.text: Map keys can be any type including objects and functions, and it preserves insertion order.
options.explanation: Plain object keys must be Strings or Symbols. Maps permit arbitrary keys (DOM nodes, objects, functions), provide a constant-time `.size` property, and guarantee iteration order.

options.text: Map serializes directly to JSON with `JSON.stringify()` without replacers.
options.explanation: `JSON.stringify(new Map())` outputs `{}` unless a custom replacer/to-object conversion is used.

options.text: Map uses less memory than an Object for small collections under 10 keys.
options.explanation: Plain objects typically have lower overhead for very small fixed-shape key-value pairs.

options.text: Map properties can be accessed directly using dot notation (`map.key`).
options.explanation: Map elements must be accessed via `.get(key)` and `.set(key, value)`.

questions.body: Why are `WeakMap` keys required to be objects (or non-registered symbols) and not primitives?
questions.keyPoints: WeakMap holds weak references to keys allowing garbage collection when no other references exist.

options.text: To allow garbage collection of the key and its associated value when no other references to the key exist.
options.explanation: WeakMap holds 'weak' references to key objects. If no other strong references to a key object exist, the key and its value can be garbage collected, preventing memory leaks.

options.text: Because primitive values have variable memory footprints that cannot be hashed.
options.explanation: Primitives have fixed memory footprints; the restriction is purely for garbage collection semantics.

options.text: To enable iteration over keys using `for...of` loops.
options.explanation: WeakMap is explicitly non-iterable because garbage collection is non-deterministic.

options.text: Because WeakMap stores its keys in local browser storage.
options.explanation: WeakMap is purely an in-memory runtime data structure.

questions.body: What does a generator function return when called, and what interface does that object implement?
questions.keyPoints: Calling a generator function returns a Generator object implementing both Iterable and Iterator protocols.

options.text: It returns a Generator object that satisfies both the `Iterable` and `Iterator` protocols (`[Symbol.iterator]` and `next()`).
options.explanation: Calling `function* ()` does not execute the body immediately; it returns a Generator object with `.next()`, `.return()`, and `.throw()` methods that also implements `[Symbol.iterator]`.

options.text: It returns a Promise that resolves with the first `yield` value.
options.explanation: Async generators involve promises, but standard generators are synchronous iterable objects.

options.text: It returns the final evaluated return value of the function synchronously.
options.explanation: Execution is paused at the beginning until `.next()` is called.

options.text: It returns an array containing all yielded values pre-calculated.
options.explanation: Generators evaluate lazily on-demand per `next()` invocation.

questions.body: What happens if a derived class constructor in ES6 fails to invoke `super()` before accessing `this`?
questions.keyPoints: In derived constructors, this is uninitialized until super() is called; accessing this throws ReferenceError.

options.text: A ReferenceError is thrown.
options.explanation: In derived class constructors, the subclass `this` binding is uninitialized until `super()` has executed. Accessing `this` beforehand throws a `ReferenceError`.

options.text: `this` defaults to the parent prototype object.
options.explanation: `this` cannot be accessed before `super()`.

options.text: The JavaScript runtime automatically calls `super()` with zero arguments silently.
options.explanation: Automatic `super()` call only occurs if no constructor is defined in the subclass at all.

options.text: A TypeError is thrown during compilation.
options.explanation: It produces a runtime `ReferenceError`.

questions.body: In a tagged template literal `tag`Hello ${name}, you have ${count} items!``, what is the first argument received by the `tag` function?
questions.keyPoints: First parameter is an array of static string segments with a raw property.

options.text: An array of static string pieces (with a `.raw` property) separated by the interpolated expressions.
options.explanation: The tag function receives `strings` (an array of literal text chunks: `['Hello ', ', you have ', ' items!']`) as argument 1, followed by the interpolated values.

options.text: The fully interpolated result string.
options.explanation: The tag function computes or formats the result; it receives separated strings and expressions.

options.text: An array containing only the interpolated expressions.
options.explanation: Expressions are passed as subsequent rest parameters (`...values`).

options.text: An object containing key-value mappings of expression names.
options.explanation: Arguments are positional arrays and values.

questions.body: How do JavaScript bitwise operators (such as `|`, `&`, `^`, `>>`) treat their operands?
questions.keyPoints: Operands are converted to 32-bit signed integers before performing bitwise operations.

options.text: They convert the operands into 32-bit signed integers in two's complement format.
options.explanation: JavaScript bitwise operators convert standard double-precision float operands into 32-bit signed big-endian integers before performing the calculation.

options.text: They operate directly on 64-bit IEEE 754 floating-point representations.
options.explanation: They convert to 32-bit integers first.

options.text: They convert operands to 16-bit unsigned Unicode character codes.
options.explanation: Bitwise operators use 32-bit signed integers.

options.text: They require operands to be BigInt values.
options.explanation: BigInt has separate bitwise operations; standard bitwise operates on Numbers.
